findings.new: Morning mercy in declaration and experience
findings.reason: Do not imply a chronological sequence between the different psalms.

findings.new: The psalm calls God's reasonings very deep. Romans praises the depth of His wisdom and knowledge and asks who knew His mind. Both portray divine understanding through depth; Romans adds explicit questions about the limits of human understanding.
findings.reason: The explicit human-limit questions belong to Romans, not both units.

findings.new: Psalm 92 speaks of the voices of many waters, wondrous sea surges and the Lord wondrous on high. Psalm 28 describes the Lord's voice over waters and the Lord over many waters. The combination of many waters, voice language and divine majesty corresponds, with the waters' voices distinct from God's voice.
findings.reason: Voice language belongs to different agents; do not make waters audible in both.

findings.new: Personal images of a shaken foot
findings.reason: The source's conditional formulation should not be presented as an unconditional confession.

findings.new: Psalm 93 presents the shaken-foot statement conditionally and follows it with the Lord's helping mercy. Psalm 72 confesses that the feet were almost shaken while envying sinners' peace. The personal foot-instability image corresponds, with the target supplying its own occasion of envy.
findings.reason: Preserve If I said.

findings.new: Command or writing used for injustice
findings.reason: The target does not explicitly call the wicked writing an ordinance.

findings.new: The psalm questions whether a throne of lawlessness shaping toil by command can join God. Isaiah condemns writers of wickedness who turn aside the poor's judgment and exploit widows and orphans. The comparison concerns command or writing associated with injustice, without supplying a particular written ordinance to Isaiah.
findings.reason: Keep the actual command-versus-writing expressions.

findings.new: The psalm places earth's ends in God's hand and assigns Him the mountain heights. Isaiah asks who measured earth with a handful and weighed the mountains. The earth-and-mountain pairing with divine handling corresponds; possession in the psalm differs from Isaiah's measurement imagery.
findings.reason: Do not assign the target's measuring imagery to both passages.

findings.new: The psalm remembers forty years of divine vexation with the generation that strays in heart. Numbers announces forty years in the wilderness bearing sins and knowing God's anger. The stated duration, wilderness generation and divine anger provide the narrative correspondence without making every clause an exact quotation.
findings.reason: Distinguish heart-straying from geographical wandering.

findings.new: Qualities before God and in His place
findings.reason: Holiness is an explicit source quality, not a word supplied by the target.

findings.new: Psalm 97 says God's right hand and holy arm won salvation for Him. Isaiah says the Lord will uncover His holy arm before nations and the earth's ends will see salvation from God. The holy-arm and salvation combination is explicit, with achieved salvation and future manifestation distinguished.
findings.reason: Preserve the source's for-Him clause.

findings.new: Trumpets made of hammered work
findings.reason: Keep the category focused on the actual particular instrument and manufacture.

findings.new: Kingship, righteousness and preparation
findings.reason: Do not make righteousness the grammatical object of prepared in both passages.

findings.new: Psalm 98 says the King's honor loves judgment and that God prepared uprightness. Proverbs says a ruling throne is prepared with righteousness and evil is abhorrent to a king. Both connect kingship, preparation and righteous order: uprightness is prepared in the psalm, while a throne is prepared with righteousness in the proverb.
findings.reason: Preserve the distinct objects and agency of preparation.

findings.new: Psalm 98 commands bowing at God's footstool. Psalm 131 resolves to enter His dwellings and bow toward the place where His feet stood. The location associated with divine feet and the act of bowing correspond; no independent object identity is asserted for the footstool.
findings.reason: The target does not explicitly call its location low.

findings.new: The psalm names Samuel among those who called on God and were heard. The narrative reports Israel requesting his intercession, his cry for Israel and the Lord hearing him. The named person and call-and-hearing action provide the concrete narrative link; the psalm also names Moses and Aaron.
findings.reason: Avoid ambiguity between Samuel the person and the title of the narrative book.

findings.new: Personal refusal of wrongdoing and hatred of evildoers
findings.reason: The source unit does not itself describe refusing company.

findings.new: Psalm 100 says a practitioner of arrogance did not dwell in the speaker's house and a speaker of unjust things did not prosper before his eyes. Psalm 5 says an evildoer will not sojourn with God and the lawless will not remain before His eyes. The dwelling-and-before-the-eyes pattern is shared, with human household and divine presence distinguished.
findings.reason: Preserve persons as the grammatical agents rather than substituting abstract arrogance and speech.

findings.new: Both ask God not to turn His face away and join affliction with a plea to hear quickly. Psalm 101 additionally specifies the ear inclined in affliction and quick hearing when called. The shared face-affliction-hearing sequence makes the parallel particular.
findings.reason: Preserve the source's distinct affliction/ear and calling/hearing clauses.

findings.new: Bird imagery with wilderness or deserted land
findings.reason: Do not transfer the wilderness pelican's location specifically to the night raven.

findings.new: The psalm compares the speaker to a wilderness pelican and a night raven on a house site. Isaiah places birds including ravens in land destined for enduring desolation. The bird imagery and wilderness or deserted settings offer a limited poetic comparison; the source's house site is not declared identical with Isaiah's deserted land. Night raven and raven are not asserted to be identical species, nor is the sufferer's situation identified with that judgment.
findings.reason: Keep the birds, locations and poetic application distinct.

findings.new: Psalm 101 announces that the time for compassion on Zion has come. Zechariah moves from asking how long Jerusalem will lack mercy to God's promise to return in compassion and again have mercy on Zion. The shared focus is compassion for Zion and its announced arrival; Zechariah supplies the explicit preceding complaint and its stated year.
findings.reason: The source does not explicitly state the target's preceding withholding of mercy.

findings.new: The psalm says God's servants took pleasure in Zion's stones and will have compassion on her dust. Nehemiah grieves over the desolated ancestral city and asks to rebuild it. Their concern for the city's material setting supplies the comparison; stones and dust remain distinct from the narrative's tombs and burned gates.
findings.reason: Preserve the source's past taking pleasure and avoid assigning every target damage detail to the source.

findings.new: Psalm 101 anticipates nations fearing the Lord's name and all earth's kings His glory. Psalm 137 asks all earth's kings to thank Him for heard words and to sing in His ways because His glory is great. The shared worldwide royal response to divine glory takes different forms: fear in the source and song in the target.
findings.reason: Keep the target's heard-words/thanks and glory/song clauses distinct.

findings.new: Regard for prayer and hearing of the needy
findings.reason: Preserve looked upon versus heard instead of assigning hearing to both units.

findings.new: Groaning prisoners and the sons of those put to death
findings.reason: The actual expression says put to death, not merely condemned.
